Crested larks (Galerida cristata) exhibit a reproductive strategy typical of many open-country passerines, with females producing multiple clutches within a single breeding season. Clutch size ranges from three to six eggs per nest [N_R_i = three to six eggs per nest], and individuals typically raise two clutches annually [F_R_i = two clutches annually]. Measured at an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which corresponds to the typical thermal conditions of their Mediterranean breeding grounds, this reproductive output represents the species' maximum capacity. Eggs weigh approximately 3.35 grams, a value derived from their dimensions of 2.27 centimeters in length and 1.68 centimeters in width, yielding a calculated mass comparable to that reported by Harr1975. This egg mass, while modest, is consistent with the allometric expectations for a passerine of this body size. The incubation period itself is relatively short, reflecting the high thermal demands of the nest environment.

Neonatal development in the Crested lark proceeds rapidly once incubation begins. Eggs maintained at a constant incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after approximately 11.5 days [ab = approximately 11.5 days], a duration that is typical among small alaudids and reflects the accelerated embryogenesis permitted by stable thermal conditions. Newly hatched chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of approximately 3.0 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.0 grams], a mass that represents only a small fraction of the ultimate adult body mass. This initial weight underscores the altricial nature of the nestlings, which are entirely dependent upon biparental provisioning during the early post-hatching period. The combination of a brief incubation period and a relatively low hatchling mass suggests a trade-off between rapid development and the allocation of resources to yolk reserves, a pattern observed in many temperate-zone passerines that face intense seasonal constraints on breeding.

Juvenile development in the Crested lark is characterized by a well-defined sequence of milestones, with many events occurring at the elevated body temperature typical of active metabolic periods. At an internal temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which is maintained by the nestlings through brooding and metabolic heat production, fledging occurs approximately 12 days after hatching [tx = approximately 12 days after hatching]. This rapid achievement of flight capability is crucial for escaping ground-based predation in the open habitats this species occupies. Sexual maturity, defined as the onset of gametogenesis and gonadal swelling, is reached approximately 36 days after hatching [tp = approximately 36 days after hatching] under these same thermal conditions, a timeline that is notably shorter than the 18 to 20 days sometimes cited in the literature, though the latter figure may reflect non-brooded captive conditions rather than natural nest environments at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Puberty thus occurs well before the onset of the first breeding season.

The timing of first reproduction in the Crested lark is delayed relative to the attainment of sexual maturity, a pattern common among species that require extended territory establishment or body condition recovery. At a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a first brood is typically produced approximately 365 days after birth [tR = approximately 365 days after birth], meaning that most individuals do not breed until the spring following their hatching year. This one-year delay is ecologically significant, as it allows young birds to accumulate sufficient lipid stores and to secure a breeding territory in the competitive, open landscapes they inhabit. The interval between fledging and first reproduction thus encompasses a full annual cycle, during which juveniles undergo a complete molt and attain their adult plumage. Most individuals then attempt to breed in their second calendar year of life, contributing to the species' moderate population turnover.

Adult body mass and longevity further define the life-history strategy of Galerida cristata. The ultimate wet weight for this species is approximately 39 grams [Wwi = approximately 39 grams], a value that falls within the broader range of 37 to 55 grams reported by field guides and reflects variation due to sex, season, and local food availability. Maximum longevity under natural conditions is approximately 4,234 days [am = approximately 4,234 days], measured at an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] in the species' warm native range. This lifespan places the Crested lark among the longer-lived passerines for its body size, a trait likely linked to its relatively low annual reproductive output and the high survival costs of ground nesting. Oldest documented individuals in the wild have been recorded at ages exceeding a decade.
